blocks.title: About this page
blocks.text: Written for this site as of November 2026 for a computer science student, in the style of the other guides. Examples use Java, with Python and C++ where the languages differ. Worked numbers were checked by program. Where a vendor, a standard or a language version matters, check the official source before relying on a detail.

**Inheritance** lets a class (the **subclass**, child or derived class) acquire the fields and methods of another (the **superclass**, parent or base class) and add or change behaviour. It models an **is-a** relationship: a `Dog` *is an* `Animal`.

blocks.text:
Output: `Animal constructor: Rex`, `Dog constructor: Labrador`, `Rex eats`, `Rex fetches`, `Woof`.

### Rules to remember

- A subclass **inherits** non-private members. It does **not** inherit constructors, but its constructor must call one (`super(...)`); if you omit the call, the compiler inserts `super()` and fails if the parent has no no-argument constructor.
- **Construction runs top-down:** the parent part of the object is built before the child part.
- **`super.method()`** calls the parent's version from an overriding method.
- Java allows **single inheritance of classes** (one `extends`), but a class can implement many interfaces. Every class ultimately extends `java.lang.Object`.
- **`final`** on a class prevents extending it (`String`); on a method it prevents overriding.
- **Private** members exist in the object but are not accessible by name from the subclass.

### What a subclass can change

| Technique | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Add** | new fields and methods |
| **Override** | replace an inherited instance method with the same signature (use `@Override` so the compiler checks it) |
| **Hide** | a field or a `static` method with the same name in the subclass hides the parent's; it is *not* overriding and is resolved by the declared type |

### Overriding rules

An overriding method must have the **same name and parameter types**, a **return type** that is the same or a subtype (a **covariant return**), an access level that is **the same or wider** (you cannot reduce `public` to `protected`), and may throw only the **same or narrower checked exceptions**. A `static`, `private` or `final` method cannot be overridden.

- Constructors are not inherited; `super(...)` must be the first statement of a constructor.
- Overriding: same signature, same-or-subtype return, same-or-wider access, no new broader checked exceptions.
- Fields and static methods are **hidden**, not overridden: the declared type decides which one you get.
- `final` class = no subclasses; `final` method = no overriding.
- Java: single class inheritance + multiple interface inheritance. C++ and Python allow multiple class inheritance.
blocks.title: Inheritance one-liners
Key points
blocks.text:
- Inheritance models is-a and reuses and extends behaviour
- The parent constructor always runs first (super(...))
- Overriding needs the same signature; access may widen but not narrow
- Fields and static methods are hidden, not overridden
- Java has single class inheritance but multiple interface inheritance

**Polymorphism** ("many forms") means one name can refer to different behaviour. Java has two kinds:

| | Compile-time (static) polymorphism | Run-time (dynamic) polymorphism |
|---|---|---|
| Mechanism | **method overloading** (same name, different parameters) | **method overriding** with a superclass reference |
| Decided | by the compiler, from the **declared types** of the arguments | by the JVM, from the **actual class** of the object |
| Also called | early binding | late binding, **dynamic dispatch** |

### Dynamic dispatch

blocks.title: Zoo.java

blocks.text:
`totalArea` knows only `Shape`. You can add a `Triangle` tomorrow and `totalArea` works unchanged: this is the **open/closed principle** (Part 3) made possible by polymorphism.

**How it works.** Each class has a **virtual method table (vtable)**: an array of pointers to its instance methods. An object has a hidden pointer to its class's table. A call `s.area()` loads the object's table and jumps to the entry for `area`, so the method that runs depends on the real class. The cost is one extra indirection per call (and the JIT often removes even that when only one implementation is loaded).

### Upcasting and downcasting

- **Upcasting** (subclass reference → superclass type) is implicit and always safe: `Shape s = new Circle(1);`. Through `s` you can call only what `Shape` declares, but **overridden methods still run the Circle version**.
- **Downcasting** (back to the subclass) needs an explicit cast and is checked at run time: a wrong cast throws `ClassCastException`. Guard with `instanceof`: `if (s instanceof Circle c) { ... c.radius ... }`.

If you find yourself downcasting often, the design is probably missing a method on the superclass type.

### Overloading is decided by the declared type

blocks.title: Overloads.java

blocks.text: `describe(a)` calls the `Animal` overload even though the object is a `Dog`, because overload selection uses the **declared (static) type**. Only overriding is resolved by the object's real type. Interview questions on this exact point are very common.
blocks.title: Gotcha: overloading is not polymorphism in the run-time sense

blocks.text: ### Fields are not polymorphic

blocks.title: FieldHiding.java
Key points
blocks.text:
- Overloading: compile time, declared types; overriding: run time, actual class (dynamic dispatch)
- A vtable per class lets a call find the right method through one indirection
- Upcasting is implicit and safe; downcasting is checked at run time and can throw ClassCastException
- Overloaded methods are chosen by the static type of the argument
- Fields and static methods are not polymorphic

An **abstract class** cannot be instantiated and may contain **abstract methods** (declared without a body) that subclasses must implement. It can also have fields, constructors and concrete methods. An **interface** describes a **contract**: a set of methods a class promises to provide, without any state.

blocks.title: Contracts.java

blocks.text:
### Abstract class or interface?

| | Abstract class | Interface |
|---|---|---|
| Instantiable | no | no |
| State (instance fields) | **yes** | no (only constants) |
| Constructors | yes | no |
| Methods | abstract and concrete, any access | abstract; `default`, `static` and `private` allowed |
| A class can extend / implement | **one** | **many** |
| Models | a partial implementation shared by related classes (**is-a**, with shared code) | a **capability or role** that unrelated classes can have (**can-do**: `Comparable`, `Runnable`) |
| Evolution | adding a method breaks nothing if it is concrete | adding a `default` method keeps old implementers working |

**Guideline:** start with an **interface** for the public contract (it leaves the single inheritance slot free and is easy to mock in tests). Add an **abstract class** only when subclasses really share state or a skeleton algorithm. A **functional interface** has exactly one abstract method and can be implemented by a lambda: `Comparator`, `Runnable`, `Function`.

### Multiple inheritance and the diamond problem

If a class inherits the **same method from two parents**, which one wins? C++ allows multiple class inheritance and needs `virtual` inheritance to avoid duplicating the shared base. Python resolves it with the **method resolution order (MRO)**, a linearisation computed by the C3 algorithm. Java avoids state conflicts by allowing only one class parent, but interfaces with `default` methods can still collide, and the compiler **forces you to resolve it**:

blocks.title: Diamond.java

blocks.text:
### Sealed hierarchies

A **sealed** class or interface lists exactly which classes may extend it, so the compiler can check a `switch` over it is **exhaustive**:

blocks.title: Shapes.java

blocks.text: Yes, when subclasses need shared **state** (instance fields), constructors, or non-public members. Interfaces cannot hold instance state. Use an interface for the contract and an abstract class (implementing it) when you also want to share fields and a skeleton algorithm.
blocks.title: Interview angle: Since Java 8 interfaces can have default methods. Are abstract classes still needed?
Key points
blocks.text:
- An abstract class can have state and constructors but a class extends only one
- An interface is a contract: no instance state, a class can implement many
- Default methods add behaviour without breaking implementers; conflicts must be resolved explicitly
- Template method: the abstract class fixes the algorithm and subclasses fill in steps
- Sealed types give exhaustive switches
- C++ uses virtual inheritance and Python uses the MRO for the diamond problem

Inheritance is the most overused feature in OOP. It creates the **tightest possible coupling** between parent and child: the child depends on how the parent works internally. **Composition** (a class *has a* reference to another and **delegates** to it) is usually more flexible.

### The fragile base class problem

blocks.title: FragileBase.java

blocks.text:
The subclass worked only until you knew that `HashSet.addAll` calls `add`. A later version of the library could change that and silently change your count: the subclass depended on an **implementation detail** of its parent. Composition depends only on the **public contract**.

### When inheritance is right

Use inheritance when it is truly **is-a**, the parent was **designed for extension** (documented, with stable hooks), and substitution is always valid. Otherwise prefer composition plus an interface:

| Question | If yes |
|---|---|
| Is the child really a special kind of the parent, in every context? | inheritance may be fine |
| Do you want to reuse code only? | use composition (delegate) |
| Might the behaviour need to change at run time? | composition (swap the delegate: the **Strategy** pattern, Part 3) |
| Do you extend a class you do not control or that was not designed for it? | avoid inheritance |

### The Liskov substitution principle (LSP)

Anywhere a parent is expected, a child must work **without surprising the caller**. The classic violation: a `Square extends Rectangle`. A rectangle lets you set width and height independently; a square cannot, so code that sets width 4 and height 5 and expects an area of 20 gets 25 from a square. Geometry says a square is a rectangle; **behaviour** says it is not a substitutable one. Part 3 covers LSP with the other SOLID principles.

- You only need to reuse some behaviour, not model a true is-a.
- The parent class was not designed for extension (most library classes).
- Behaviour should change at run time (swap the delegate).
- You would inherit methods that make no sense for the child (`Stack extends Vector` exposes `insertElementAt`).
- Rule: *favour composition over inheritance*, and design classes either **for** extension (documented) or **forbid** it (`final`).
blocks.title: Prefer composition when
Key points
blocks.text:
- Inheritance couples a child to the parent's implementation; composition couples to its public contract
- The fragile base class problem: a subclass breaks when the parent changes internally
- Use inheritance only for a true is-a that is safe in every context
- Liskov: a subtype must be usable wherever the parent is expected, without surprises
- Delegate instead of inherit when you want reuse or run-time flexibility

15 original questions on 14 areas. *Recall* questions test a definition or a rule. *Problem* questions give you numbers or a short scenario to work out. Pick an answer to see why it is right and which trap catches people.

o: it does not compile because of the call with null
items.w: Overloads are chosen from the declared types. `o` is declared Object, so the Object version runs. The literal is a String. For `null`, both overloads apply and the compiler picks the most specific one, String.
`sound` is an overridden instance method, so the version chosen depends on the actual class of the object at run time: Dog's for the first call, Animal's for the second.
Static methods are hidden, not overridden, and the call is bound at compile time using the declared type of x, which is A. So A.name() runs.
Fields are not polymorphic. The field accessed is the one of the declared type: `p.name` is P's field ("parent") and after the cast `((C) p).name` is C's field ("child").
Each constructor implicitly starts with `super()`, so construction runs from the top of the hierarchy down: A, then B, then C.

HashSet.addAll is implemented by calling add() for each element, so every element is counted once in addAll and once more in the overridden add: 3 + 3 = 6. The subclass relied on an implementation detail of its parent, the fragile base class problem.

items.q: *(Recall)* Which keyword prevents a method from being overridden in subclasses?
items.w: A `final` method cannot be overridden. `abstract` requires overriding, `static` methods are hidden rather than overridden, and `sealed` restricts which classes may extend a type.

o: interfaces, but a class extends only one class
items.w: A Java class can extend one class and implement many interfaces. This avoids the state ambiguity of multiple class inheritance.

o: a class should have only one reason to change
subclasses must override every method of the parent
objects of a subclass should be usable wherever objects of the superclass are expected, without breaking the program's correctness
classes should depend on abstractions, not on concrete classes
items.w: LSP concerns behavioural substitutability of subtypes. Option (b) describes the single responsibility principle and (c) the dependency inversion principle.

blocks.text: #### Inheritance

items.question: Why must the first line of a subclass constructor call a parent constructor?
items.answer: The parent's part of the object must be initialised before the child's part, which may depend on it. If you write no call, the compiler inserts `super()`; if the parent has no no-argument constructor you must call one explicitly.

items.question: What is the difference between overriding and hiding?
items.answer: Overriding replaces an instance method, and the version that runs is chosen at run time from the object's actual class. Hiding applies to fields and static methods: the version used is chosen at compile time from the declared type of the reference.

blocks.text: #### Polymorphism

items.question: What does `Animal a = new Dog(); a.who();` call, and what decides it?
items.answer: It calls `Dog.who()` if Dog overrides it. Instance methods are dispatched dynamically using the actual class of the object, not the declared type of the reference.

items.question: How does the JVM implement run-time polymorphism cheaply?
items.answer: Each class has a virtual method table of its instance methods and each object points to its class. A call indexes the table to find the method to run, which costs one extra indirection, and the JIT compiler can often inline the call when only one implementation exists.

blocks.text: #### Abstract classes and interfaces

items.question: Why does Java not allow multiple inheritance of classes?
items.answer: It avoids the ambiguity and complexity of the diamond problem: two parents with their own fields and methods of the same name. Java gets the benefit of multiple inheritance through interfaces, which carry no instance state, and the compiler makes the programmer resolve any default-method conflict.

items.question: When would you choose an abstract class over an interface?
items.answer: When the related subclasses share state or a partly implemented algorithm (fields, constructors, concrete methods, protected helpers). An interface suits a capability that unrelated classes can implement.

blocks.text: #### Composition over inheritance

items.question: What is the fragile base class problem?
items.answer: A subclass relies on how its parent works internally, for example that `addAll` calls `add`. If the parent's implementation changes, the subclass can break even though the parent's public contract is unchanged. Composition avoids it by depending only on the contract.

items.question: Why is Square extends Rectangle a classic violation of the Liskov substitution principle?
items.answer: A Rectangle promises that width and height can be set independently. A Square must keep them equal, so code written for Rectangles (set width 4, height 5, expect area 20) gives the wrong answer with a Square. The subtype changes behaviour that callers rely on.
